overview: The Medford City Council is the legislative body for the City of Medford, responsible for enacting ordinances, adopting the municipal budget, allocating property tax rates, authorizing appropriations and loan orders, and approving licenses and zoning changes. The council has been meeting across the 2024–2025 and 2026–2027 terms, spanning September 2024 through September 2026. Over this time, the body has enacted comprehensive zoning overhauls for commercial corridors, approved major financing packages for school facilities and lead pipe replacements, and updated municipal policies on surveillance and compensation. At its most recent meetings, the council has been managing recurring budgetary disputes with the administration regarding legal spending while advancing inclusionary housing adjustments, capital appropriations, and neighborhood ward meetings.

threads.name: Comprehensive corridor and district rezoning
threads.summary: The council undertook an extensive overhaul of city zoning codes and district definitions across multiple commercial and neighborhood corridors. It referred and ultimately ordained rezoning for the Mystic Avenue Corridor District with affordable housing incentives and ground-floor commercial rules, followed by the Salem Street corridor, where the Salem and Park Street node was revised from MX2 to MX1. In 2026, the council ordained major overhauls for the Medford Square District and the Boston Avenue Neighborhood Corridor District, including allowances for student housing. Most recently, the council ordained an inclusionary housing amendment allowing fractional cash payments to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund and referred a draft request for proposals for zoning consultants to committee.

threads.name: Municipal charter revision
threads.summary: Following earlier study committee work, the council reviewed recommendations and prepared a comprehensive revision of the Medford City Charter. In March and April 2025, the council debated and approved a draft hybrid city charter with amendments addressing periodic review timelines and the mayor's role on the School Committee, submitting the finalized draft to the mayor and the state legislature. In October 2025, the council approved a resolution calling for a citywide public information campaign before the charter reform ballot question went before voters in November. Discussions regarding the implementation of the new charter and council procedures were referred to committee in February 2026.

threads.name: Values-Aligned Local Investments Ordinance and litigation
threads.summary: The council debated an ethical divestment ordinance barring municipal investment in fossil fuels, private prisons, weapons manufacturers, and human rights violators, drawing substantial public testimony. After advancing through initial readings, the council enacted the ordinance on third reading in September 2025 and subsequently voted to override the mayor's veto in November 2025. Following a federal lawsuit challenging the ordinance, Chertok v. City of Medford, the council requested $75,000 from the mayor to fund its legal defense. By September 2026, the council adopted a formal declaration supporting legal intervention in the federal lawsuit by residents or the state Attorney General.

threads.name: Law department oversight and legal spending dispute
threads.summary: Prompted by rising municipal litigation and unfair labor practice charges, the council approved a resolution in February 2026 seeking an independent review and a comprehensive report on legal expenses since 2019. After the administration failed to deliver the report, the council voted in April 2026 to submit a formal public records request, followed by an appeal to the state Public Records Division in June. Concurrently, the council cut the Law Department's fiscal year 2027 budget by 83 percent, requiring the administration to seek supplemental monthly appropriations. In September 2026, the council approved only a one-month supplemental funding extension through October while continuing to press for legal spending documentation.

threads.name: School and municipal infrastructure financing
threads.summary: The council regularly authorized substantial funding packages for school buildings, lead pipe remediation, and municipal facilities. Beginning in late 2024, the body authorized borrowing for school HVAC work and lead line replacement, culminating in a $30.7 million combined financing package for the McGlynn and Andrews schools in April 2025. Councilors allocated millions from free cash and capital stabilization funds to water main replacements and Massachusetts School Building Authority feasibility studies for Roberts, Missituk, and Brooks Elementary Schools. In September 2026, the council approved stabilization appropriations of $1.3 million for road resurfacing and $1 million for Hormel Stadium turf replacement.

threads.name: Surveillance and civil liberties policies
threads.summary: The council repeatedly addressed surveillance technology and resident privacy through ordinance amendments and policy votes. Between December 2024 and January 2025, the body amended the Community Control Over Public Surveillance Ordinance to restrict the purchase of bulk commercial surveillance data and regulate the disposal of improperly gathered records. In May 2025, the council approved the annual surveillance report and parking department license plate reader policies. The council then introduced and enacted a standalone ordinance prohibiting municipal acquisition, possession, or use of face surveillance technology, passing its third and final reading in April 2026.

threads.name: Medford Square parking lot redevelopment
threads.summary: Community members raised early concerns in October 2024 over preserving parking access for Senior Center visitors during the planned redevelopment behind City Hall. In May 2025, the city designated Transom Real Estate as the preferred developer to negotiate a long-term lease for the Medford Square parking lots. In March 2026, the council took a regulatory vote declaring the parcels surplus and authorizing a 99-year ground lease to Transom Real Estate, subsequently referring and adopting a Medford Square City Hall Overlay District. The council also accepted a $450,000 state grant in May 2026 to support archaeological and excavation work on the redevelopment site.

threads.name: Tree protection and urban canopy management
threads.summary: Efforts to safeguard Medford's urban forest began with committee reviews of public and private tree regulations in late 2024. In November 2025, the council ordained an ordinance creating a volunteer tree committee to support the tree warden, followed shortly by the acceptance of a $25,000 private donation from Trees Medford for plantings. In mid-2026, the council restructured DPW personnel by raising the pay grade and hours of the Tree Warden to lead the DPW Forestry Division. Finally, in September 2026, the council ordained the Public Tree Ordinance to establish binding management and preservation standards for trees on municipal land.
